claims.claim: A written WotC house style guide exists — 'D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing' v1.04a (©2013), built on Chicago 16 and Merriam-Webster 11 — and it governs typography, numerals, verb collocations, capitalization and tone, with no rule at all on boxed/read-aloud text.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing

claims.claim: A later revision, v1.08a (©2018, circulated as 'updated January 2019'), keeps the same structure (Chicago 17 now) and adds headings hierarchy, sidebar, gender-suffix, 'fellowship vs party' and edition-naming rules; it still contains nothing on boxed text or read-aloud prose.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: Avoid overusing sidebars.

claims.claim: The style guide was released publicly on DMs Guild around October 2018 as one of four free PDFs (IP guide, adventure guide, style guide, Forgotten Realms guide) that had previously gone only to official-play writers.
claims.source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

claims.claim: On 2019-02-22 the DMs Guild account announced an updated House Style Guide listing for creators, noting it adds tips on gender-neutral language.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'Creators: Style Guide is now on DMsGuild!' (@dms_guild, 2019-02-22)
claims.quote: An updated #DnD House Style Guide is now on #DMsGuild

claims.claim: The Kind GM's post on the creator resource carries a May 2020 commenter report that the material was no longer available, which the author acknowledged — so the public window was roughly 2018–2020.
claims.source: The Kind GM — DMs Guild Style Guide Resources (2018-10-24)

claims.feature: house style guide (community says none published)
claims.claim: Community writers on either side of that window report no official guide: Half-Cover (2017) says WotC 'has not yet published the official style guide', Old Dungeon Master (2015) compiled one from 3.5/4e guides ('Perhaps they have one and I just couldn't find it'), and Blog of Holding (2025) says of the 2024 rules 'it annoys me not to have an official style guide'.
claims.source: Half-Cover — How to Follow the Writing Style of D&D (Michael, 2017-09-02)
claims.quote: has not yet published the official style guide

claims.feature: house style guide (community says none published, 2024 rules)
claims.claim: Paul Hughes built an unofficial 2024 style guide because no official one for the 2024 rules is available to the public.
claims.source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)
claims.quote: it annoys me not to have an official style guide

claims.claim: Work-for-hire WotC freelancers receive the D&D House Style Guide, the 5e Word template, pitch examples and lore documents at contract start, and drafts are formatted with them.
claims.source: POCGamer — What happened? Writing for Wizards, Part 1 (Graeme Barber, 2021-03-23)

claims.claim: The official Adventurers League Dungeoncraft guide tells authors they must use the provided template and 'formatting standards as presented in the template' and be familiar with the D&D Style Guide, which it says is also provided.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Adventurers League Dungeoncraft Design Guide: The Wild Beyond the Witchlight, v1.2 (media.wizards.com)
claims.quote: You should be familiar with the D&D Style Guide

claims.claim: The 2023 Dungeoncraft Design Guide (effective 2023-11-09) again requires a specific template and familiarity with the D&D Style Guide; a poster frames this as organized play needing 'more guiderails than your usual table does'.
claims.source: EN World — D&D Adventurers League Unveils New DungeonCraft Document with Planescape In Focus (Raddu, 2023-11)
claims.quote: more guiderails than your usual table does

claims.claim: Kobold Press ran a 'Designing with Style' series that explicitly 'breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide', quoting its Common Pitfalls section verbatim — evidence the guide was public and treated as canonical by third-party 5e designers.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
claims.quote: breaks down the official 5th-edition style guide

claims.claim: The guide's stated reason for second person in rules text is gender neutrality: 'In rules text, we often achieve gender neutrality by writing in the second person.'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: writing in the second person

claims.claim: v1.04a forbids 'they'/'their' as singular pronouns except in dialogue; v1.08a reverses this 'in a departure from our past usage' but tells writers to rely on it only when no pleasing alternative exists.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: but don't abuse this liberty

claims.claim: The guide fixes the game's verb idiom in a list: you cast a spell, deal damage, make a saving throw that succeeds or fails, make an attack that hits or misses, take damage, regain hit points, score a critical hit, use a feature.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: You make a saving throw, and it succeeds or fails

claims.claim: Common Pitfalls: never write 'must make a DC 15 Strength check' unless success and failure are described next; the canonical form is 'must succeed on'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: You must succeed on a DC 15 Strength check

claims.claim: Third-party style guidance derived from the WotC guide: skill checks are always written as '[Ability Score] ([Skill])', outcomes are stated for success and failure, and multi-skill checks name at most two skills for brevity.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Designing with Style: Ability Checks and Saving Throws (Hannah Rose, 2019-05-31)
claims.quote: always written as [Ability Score] ([Skill])

claims.feature: numerals in rules vs words in narrative
claims.claim: Rules text uses numerals for any game quantity ('regains 3 hit points', 'lasts for 1 round', 'The room is 20 feet square') while narrative time and distance are spelled out ('slept for six hours', 'fifty miles apart').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: the characters slept for six hours
claims.page: v1.04a pp.5-6, Numerals in Rules Text

claims.claim: The guide explicitly retires 4e usages: 'save' as 'successful saving throw' and 'result' as 'the number rolled on a die' — 'We have abandoned that practice.'
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: We have abandoned that practice

claims.claim: Write 'deals 10 fire damage', not '10 points of fire damage'; write 'hit point maximum', not 'maximum hit points'; 'magic item' is never 'magical item'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: Avoid referring to points of damage

claims.claim: Capitalize ability scores, Armor Class, class features, Difficulty Class, feats, languages, planes, skills, racial/monster traits; italicize spell and magic-item names as titles (the spell wall of fire produces a wall of fire).
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

claims.claim: Inline subheads (heading 4) end with terminal punctuation, not a colon — 'Keen Senses. You have proficiency…' — and are set in bold italics; bolded stat-block fields are a different thing.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: followed by terminal punctuation, not a colon

claims.feature: no weeks or months in rules
claims.claim: Because a Realms week is a tenday, rules durations are given in days, never weeks or months (years are allowed).
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: say a game effect lasts for 7 days

claims.claim: The guide encourages contractions formed with 'not' (don't, can't, wasn't) and warns against ambiguous ones like 'who's' — a deliberately conversational register for rules.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

claims.claim: The only tone guidance in the guide: D&D is high fantasy about small teams; humor or tragedy is fine if it doesn't overtake the tone, tested against Lord of the Rings / Game of Thrones — 'ring wraiths aren't used for gags'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)
claims.quote: ring wraiths aren't used for gags

claims.claim: v1.08a adds a diction rule: avoid 'fellowship' for adventuring groups because D&D companies are 'often fractious or more mercenary'; use group, band, company or especially 'party'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: often fractious or more mercenary

claims.claim: v1.08a switches from '5th Edition' to lowercase 'fifth edition', preferably as a modifier ('the fifth edition Dungeon Master's Guide').
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

claims.claim: v1.08a: write 'priest', 'actor', 'god' regardless of gender; '-ess' forms only in in-world titles.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)
claims.quote: Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible

claims.claim: v1.08a requires descending the heading hierarchy without skipping levels, forbids inline subheads used merely for emphasis, and says the best sidebars 'can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense'.
claims.source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (©2018, 'updated January 2019'; PDF mirror)

claims.feature: in-world tenday rule vs WotC practice
claims.claim: A poster notes the style guide bans 'week' in favor of 'tenday' while WotC's own hardcovers violate the rule — house style is aspirational, not uniformly applied.
claims.source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

claims.claim: Half-Cover infers from the books that spells and saving throws use 'very specific wording' and that features always spell out interactions (e.g., already having a cantrip), with fixed section order (starting equipment before class features).
claims.source: Half-Cover — How to Follow the Writing Style of D&D (Michael, 2017-09-02)
claims.quote: a strict style guide that all D&D sections adhere to

claims.claim: A community-compiled 5e writer's guide: 'Write in the present tense', avoiding 'will' for NPC/monster actions ('the golem attacks').
claims.source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5E Writer's Guide (Ronny, 2015-08-03)
claims.quote: Wherever possible, avoid using the future tense

claims.claim: In 2024 text, Bonus Action, Advantage/Disadvantage, Hit Points, Armor Class, Death Saving Throw, Proficiency Bonus, Challenge Rating and D20 Test are capitalized while ability, action, saving throw, skill, spell and feat stay lowercase; monster-name capitalization is inconsistent.
claims.source: Blog of Holding — Unofficial D&D 2024 Style Guide (Paul Hughes, 2025-01-07)

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 2024 capitalizes defined terms (Cone, Target) to flag Rules Glossary entries, but definitions then live only in the glossary, scattering the targeting rules across pp. 236–238, 361, 364 and 376.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — D&D 5E 2024: Why Rules Glossaries Kinda Suck (2024-08-28)

claims.claim: 2024 condition text is standardized to mechanical statements — 'Your Speed is 0 and can't increase' replaces 2014's 'can't move' — and 'Utilize', 'Study', 'Influence' and 'D20 Test' become defined capitalized terms.
claims.source: Dungeon Master Assistance — D&D 5.5 PHB Review: Playing the Game and the Rules Glossary (Ronny, 2024-10-01)
claims.quote: Your Speed is 0 and can't increase

claims.feature: teach-first structure and annotated play example (2024)
claims.claim: The 2024 PHB opens with a How to Play chapter and a two-column example of play annotated with the applicable rules; Crawford frames the rewrite as 'teaching you how to play', contrasting 2014 which 'jumps right into character creation'.
claims.source: Wargamer — New DnD Player's Handbook aims to actually teach you the game (2024-06-18)
claims.quote: teaching you how to play

claims.claim: Idle Cartulary judges the 48-page rules section plus 18-page glossary 'absolutely stellar information design' and 'an incredibly confident book', though terms like Influence action lack definition where used.
claims.source: Idle Cartulary (Playful Void) — I Read The Player's Handbook (2024) (2024-08-31)
claims.quote: absolutely stellar information design

claims.claim: Mearls' 2013 Legends & Lore argument, as quoted: feat names like 'Rapid Shot and Precise Shot are abstract things that aren't really clear', whereas describing a fighter as an archer 'makes sense to anyone'; rules are 'a shared language'.
claims.source: Tenkar's Tavern — Mike Mearls' Latest Legends & Lore Column: Where Less is More (2013-03-03)
claims.quote: a shared language

claims.claim: A 2014 EN World thread infers that 5e designers chose rulings over exact language, which lets them 'use more natural language' — community inference from Mearls' videos, not a designer statement about prose.
claims.source: EN World — Design Philosophy of 5e (thread, 2014-06-25)
claims.quote: use more natural language

claims.claim: 5e core-book editor Scott Fitzgerald Gray: mechanics editing needs precision in how a book 'fits in with the game as a whole', narrative editing needs flow and pacing, and prose editing serves 'the emotional language of the game' so readers feel like a character in the world.
claims.source: Shadomain — Tales From the Tavern: Interview with Scott Fitzgerald Gray (2024-03-20)
claims.quote: the emotional language of the game

claims.claim: Perkins says every adventure for a decade had to re-explain doors, so the 2024 DMG codifies them; Wyatt calls re-explaining boxed text in every adventure a 'stupid little thing' the DMG (p. 9) now covers, pending the editing team.
claims.source: Screen Rant — After DM's Guide Preview, I'm Convinced Future D&D Adventures Will Drop These Two Repetitive Features (Ben Brosofsky, 2024-10-29)
claims.quote: stupid little thing

claims.claim: Perkins on the 2024 DMG: 'everything in there better be cracking on topic'; the sample adventures use 'tight and short' read-aloud scripts to jog the DM's memory, avoiding his earlier 32-page adventures.
claims.source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: tight and short

claims.feature: Curse of Strahd vs Storm King's Thunder boxed text
claims.claim: DMDavid observes Perkins boxed every location in Curse of Strahd, even empty rooms, and that his next adventure, Storm King's Thunder, 'omits almost all read-aloud text' — the two extremes of WotC 5e practice.
claims.source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
claims.quote: omits almost all read-aloud text

claims.claim: Every 2025 MM entry opens with a single characterizing phrase ('tentacled subterranean trapper', 'guardian manifestation of the divine'); lore is 'compact but effective' though 'a little too compact for my taste'; quote boxes appear on some entries.
claims.source: EN World — Monsters & More: An In-Depth Review of the 2025 D&D Monster Manual (Beth Rimmels, 2025-01-28)
claims.quote: tentacled subterranean trapper

claims.claim: TheGamer: 'The flavor has amped up narratively, and the mechanics have followed' (angels wield light, kenku use shadow-magic daggers); there is no lore glossary.
claims.source: TheGamer — 2025 Monster Manual Review (Jerel Levy, 2025-01-28)

claims.claim: Xanathar's Guide carries 'little notes that run as commentary throughout the book, usually a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter', continuing the Volo's device but less relevant on a mechanics-heavy book.
claims.source: Skyland Games — Review: Xanathar's Guide to Everything (Scott D, 2017-11-13)
claims.quote: a sort of joke or snipe about the subject matter

claims.claim: Dyson Logos, citing Decker and Noonan's 2005 GenCon table observations, holds that a DM gets two sentences before players stack dice; players missed dimensions, exits and monster counts in longer boxed text.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
claims.quote: you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: A 2025 EN World poster re-cites the 2005 Noonan/Decker WotC article: two sentences, 'DMs who didn't used boxed text had more engagement', cold reading is worse than personal phrasing, 'Ditch the boxed text and use your own words' — upstream article not fetched, single-lineage claim.
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
claims.quote: Ditch the boxed text and use your own words

claims.claim: Thread posters set ceilings of 'no more than two sentences' (GM Lent) or '3 to 5 sentences at most' with listed details for closer investigation (el-remmen).
claims.source: EN World — Read aloud text in modules: What are folks' opinions? (thread, page 4, 2025-04-05)
claims.quote: 3 to 5 sentences at most

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin's D&D Beyond craft column: an opening should be 'Four sentences, and less than 100 words'; avoid 'paragraph after paragraph of boxed text'.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words

claims.claim: A 5e designer describes evolving from verbose 5e style to bullets to boxed text that is 'typically three lines, and never longer than five' because it sped play and set a base tone per room.
claims.source: Revivify Games — What I Value In Adventure Design (2025-03-04)
claims.quote: typically three lines, and never longer than five

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: a read-aloud is a tiny story told in 'less than 250 words'; if editing didn't remove 25% you didn't try; 'Keep it short and keep it powerful.'
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: less than 250 words to tell it

claims.claim: Outside introductions, a boxed text with a paragraph break 'isn't already too long by half' is rare; villain dialogue should be broken into ~six-second (one-round) statements.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
claims.quote: isn't already too long by half

claims.claim: Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long'; break 'freeze-frame' text into actionable chunks and stop at the reaction point so players respond before the world moves on.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
claims.quote: boxed text is often too long

claims.claim: Gus L.: a basic room key is five sentences maximum; longer only for puzzles and NPCs — 'no one wants to read a three page key'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: no one wants to read a three page key

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch: long read-aloud at each location means 'the players are almost certainly going to be playing with their phones', even when, rarely, the prose is good.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)

claims.feature: third person over second person in boxed text
claims.claim: Merwin's core fix: 'Move from the second-person point of view to the third person' — 'The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center of this small clearing' instead of 'As you enter the clearing, you notice…' — so text cannot dictate PC actions or feelings.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Move from the second-person point of view to the third person

claims.feature: no dictated PC actions or emotions
claims.claim: Merwin's D&D Beyond rules: never 'as you approach' or 'you enter'; never 'stunned', 'terrified', 'heart pounds'; no game-mechanics terms used non-mechanically in boxed text.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)

claims.claim: Alexander names the pitfall 'remote-control text': 'You step forward', 'You smile', or declaring 'the thoughts or feelings' of PCs; show the scene, 'don't tell them how they're reacting to it'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
claims.quote: the thoughts or feelings

claims.claim: Dyson: bad boxed text 'predicts the future for the party (upon approaching…)' or commands behavior ('you stand in shock'); cure is one or two simple sentences or a point-form list.
claims.source: Dyson's Dodecahedron — The Dreaded Boxed Text (Dyson Logos, 2013-09-29)
claims.quote: predicts the future for the party

claims.claim: DM's Workshop argues the opposite of Merwin: shift from third-person objective ('A 200-foot waterfall cascades') to second-person subjective ('You see a majestic waterfall') so the DM addresses the players rather than 'the empty air'.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
claims.quote: the empty air

claims.claim: Key-writing rule: 'Write without assumption of perspective' about entry point; use compass directions ('east wall'), never relative ones ('far side').
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)
claims.quote: Write without assumption of perspective

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: keep descriptions 'short and punchy', don't tell players what to feel, use east/west not left/right, and let the map carry redundant door descriptions.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)
claims.quote: short and punchy

claims.claim: Readers summarizing Lynch's standards: don't provide conclusions, avoid 'if/then' constructs as padding, and don't address the party directly in read-aloud.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)

claims.claim: Robin D. Laws: in hypothetical RPG text drop 'will' — 'If the agents reach the safe house, Keletny burns the car'; also avoid passive voice and 'to be' + verb pairs.
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)
claims.quote: Keletny burns the car

claims.claim: Ray Vallese's editor's guide devotes a section to 'using present tense instead of future tense' and to 'avoiding rampant capitalization' — two habits of RPG manuscripts an editor corrects.
claims.source: Ray Vallese — Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers (book page)
claims.quote: using present tense instead of future tense

claims.feature: describe what can be sensed, not what can't
claims.claim: Merwin's epistemic rule: 'Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot' — no crate contents, but never omit the 50-foot chasm.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Describe everything the characters can sense, but not what they cannot

claims.claim: Words like 'seems' and 'appears' telegraph tricks: 'If something "appears to be" to the characters, it "is"' — let Perception checks, not hedges, create the distinction.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: If something 'appears to be' to the characters, it 'is'

claims.claim: Include only environmental details PCs will interact with; the smell of flowers can go 'unless you happen to be DMing for a party comprised solely of elves or florists'.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: a party comprised solely of elves or florists

claims.claim: 'Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge': no evil soliloquies, no coronation cutscenes; keep passages short and let PCs act.
claims.source: Critical Hits — Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2010-08-27)
claims.quote: Avoid the novelist/dramatist urge

claims.claim: 'Read your boxed text aloud to check readability' — tongue-twisters, unintended alliteration and odd phrasing are invisible on the page.
claims.source: D&D Beyond — Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, 2019-11-06)
claims.quote: Read your boxed text aloud to check readability

claims.claim: Lynch's most-cited rule as summarized: replace the abstract judgment ('a cruel bully') with the concrete action ('Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll'); aim for 'the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait'; specificity, not mere detail.
claims.source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)
claims.quote: the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait

claims.claim: tenfootpole grades language on a four-point scale topped by 'Succinct and evocative', lists 'Terse writing style' and 'Evocative atmosphere' as requirements, and states 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing'.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Review Standards (Bryce Lynch)
claims.quote: Succinct and evocative

claims.claim: Lynch praises one 5e read-aloud for avoiding 'the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud' and for capturing a social scene in progress.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — (5e) Death in the Wood review (Bryce Lynch, 2019-02-09)
claims.quote: the overwritten fantasy drivil that is present in most read aloud

claims.claim: Skerples: use find-and-replace to hunt filler words ('little, big, grand, tall, dark') and swap in evocative choices; 'Every sentence needs to fight for its life in a dungeon key.'
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Every sentence needs to fight for its life

claims.claim: Gus L.: not 'evil idol' but 'toothy glare' or 'sharp edged obsidian'; include non-visual senses but never room history, future or emotions.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: sharp edged obsidian

claims.claim: Celeste Conowitch: 'keep it simple with a few powerful details' — the facts plus one detail ('reeks of garlic') that gives the room a story; never name the monster in narration.
claims.source: Kobold Press — Run your best actual play: Paint Me a Picture (Celeste Conowitch, 2026-07-20)
claims.quote: keep it simple with a few powerful details

claims.claim: Alexander's room formula: list notable things with positions, tag them with three of the five senses ('Try to include three of them'), then add a verb; NPCs get an action, clothing and one trait — 'you're not describing their headshot'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — Random GM Tip: Description Formulas (2022-02-08)
claims.quote: Try to include three of them

claims.claim: Anne K. Brown's essay (as reported): use all five senses and show rather than tell ('you detect orcs' is the failure), but don't over-invest in sensory prose players can't use.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.page: report on Brown, 'Listen! Do You Smell Something?'

claims.claim: Chris Doyle's essay (as reported): write read-aloud like a newspaper lead — immediate threat first ('GIANT SLAVERING OGRE'), secondary details after, lower-level details left for searching.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.quote: GIANT SLAVERING OGRE
claims.page: report on Doyle, 'How to Write Encounters that Don't Suck'

claims.claim: Sly Flourish: use fantastical language — 'quit writing read-aloud text that sounds like it came from Ikea instructions' — and make sure 'every word has a place in it'.
claims.source: Sly Flourish — Writing Awesome Read-Aloud Text (Mike Shea, 2010-11-08)
claims.quote: sounds like it came from Ikea instructions

claims.feature: punchy, emotionally slanted commercial boxed text
claims.claim: A review of dScryb's commercial boxed text finds it 'very punchy and to the point', carrying 'emotional information, motivations, or default assumptions' and sometimes 'selling' the creature or place.
claims.source: Gnome Stew — dScryb First Impressions (Rascher, 2021-07)
claims.quote: very punchy and to the point

claims.feature: active voice and expletive cuts (editor via critic)
claims.claim: Vallese's book, per Lynch: cut 'there is/are' openings ('An old wise man watches over the children'), prefer active constructions, and reorder stacked modifiers ('Its wormlike body is thin and scaly').
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: Its wormlike body is thin and scaly

claims.claim: Vallese: 'Do you have to follow all of these tips all the time? Nope… Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them' — vary to keep flavor and voice.
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Review: Writing with Style (J.T. Evans, 2017-10-23)
claims.quote: Just be sure you understand the rules before you break them

claims.claim: Laws' fifth key: use plurals to dodge gendered pronouns — 'Characters can leave their pistols at the door.'
claims.source: Pelgrane Press — Five Keys to Punchier Prose (Robin D. Laws, 2012-02-01)
claims.quote: Characters can leave their pistols at the door

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 7: replace 'to be' verbs with active ones and show rather than tell — describe details that reveal information through play.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)

claims.claim: Merwin prefers the term 'narrative text': 'a series of prompts that can help your game flow more smoothly'; 'Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting' for atmosphere.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'This is exactly why boxed text is important' (Shawn Merwin, 2021-11)
claims.quote: Excellent boxed text does a lot of heavy lifting

claims.claim: Merwin (2019): 'A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text (well-written hopefully)' — omitting it is 'a risk', even though streamers rarely read it.
claims.source: D&D Sage Advice (sageadvice.eu) — 'What are your thoughts on boxed text?' (Shawn Merwin tweet, 2019-04-14)
claims.quote: A majority of DMs out there WANT boxed text

claims.claim: Alexander rejects 3e's Traps/Creatures/Tactics/Development/Treasure key format because writers 'fill the format' and information lands out of play sequence: the ogre in the middle comes first, the goblin behind the tapestry does not.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key (2014)
claims.quote: fill the format

claims.claim: The essential key: room title, boxed text ('seen in a glance'), reactive checks front-loaded, bold-titled significant elements, developing details from general to specific, a GM-background tag — and 'Complete sentences are overrated'.
claims.source: The Alexandrian — The Art of the Key, Part 2: The Essential Key (2014-05-21)
claims.quote: Complete sentences are overrated

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons: first paragraph describes 'everything immediately observable' with interactables in bold; list contents in the order described; monsters go last in the first description but first in later keying.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)
claims.quote: Write a paragraph that describes everything immediately observable

claims.claim: Gus L.: '3 or 4 bolded words maximum' per complex room, each keyed to a follow-up paragraph; start with the room's inhabitants, then dangers, valuables, then hidden items tagged '(trap)' or '(hidden)'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: 3 or 4 bolded words maximum

claims.claim: BAATAG rule 2: no bullets or bolding by default — 'Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents'; later paragraphs are one topic each, recognizable from the first few words.
claims.source: Being An Asshole To A Goblin — Elements of a Key 4: Rules for Key-Writing (Misha F, 2026-04-28)
claims.quote: Plain text paragraphs still need to serve as reference documents

claims.claim: Cygnus's rewrite format: name, a 1–2 sentence description touching several senses ('what the characters can immediately perceive'), listed interactables, nested details, stat lines last — explicitly to avoid long boxed text.
claims.source: The Lady and Tiger — Rewriting Dungeon Keys (Cygnus, 2023-11-30)
claims.quote: what the characters can immediately perceive

claims.claim: Tad Davis describes Campbell's economy method: bold for immediately visible items, arrows to hidden ones, indentation for stacking, omitting non-essential words, with sound/smell/breeze cues.
claims.source: ars phantasia — On Useful Dungeon Key Entries (Tad Davis, 2013-12-05)

claims.claim: Designing Dungeons cites Courtney Campbell's target of encoding 'everything you need to run successfully in seven words'.
claims.source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)

claims.claim: Skerples: 'Cut mercilessly. Turn pages to paragraphs, paragraphs sentences, sentences to tables'; 'Sprawl is the enemy of utility'; begin with what is seen at a glance, then motion, smells, details, hidden information — never 'This room is…'.
claims.source: Coins and Scrolls — OSR: Sharpening the Axe: How I Plan and Write RPG Books (Skerples, 2019-09-05)
claims.quote: Sprawl is the enemy of utility

claims.claim: Gus L.: 'Maps! Use them.' — never spend key lines on dimensions and exits.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: Maps! Use them.

claims.claim: Gus L. rejects player-facing boxed text because it discourages referees from reading keys and is 'depreciating one big advantage RPGs have'.
claims.source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
claims.quote: depreciating one big advantage RPGs have

claims.feature: one-line keys vs the G1 pattern
claims.claim: DMDavid: Gygax 'usually wrote a 1-line note for each room' for Castle Greyhawk, but G1 (1978) gave 'generous descriptions for every location' and 'set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow'; length should match a location's purpose.
claims.source: DMDavid — How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, 2016-11-21)
claims.quote: usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: Jobe Bittman (as reported): give 'that which is necessary for the GM to run the scenario and have it make sense, and no more'.
claims.source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
claims.quote: and no more

claims.feature: subtext in adventure vs rules text
claims.claim: Monte Cook: adventure text states facts plainly and leaves the solution as subtext ('It's better unsaid'); setting text 'Don't be coy about the important stuff'; rules text never uses subtext.
claims.source: Monte Cook — Subtext in Game Writing (RPG Design Theories, 2022-12-22)
claims.quote: It's better unsaid.

claims.claim: Arnold K.: write snippets, run the dungeon to expose weaknesses, then cut — 'It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon'.
claims.source: Goblin Punch — How I Write An Adventure (Arnold K., 2017-01-27)
claims.quote: It's better to have a small, excellent dungeon

claims.claim: Lynch faults Vallese's guide for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing — the DM must 'glance at the page and immediately find' what is needed.
claims.source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
claims.quote: glance at the page and immediately find

claims.claim: Perkins describes the 2024 DMG sample adventures' read-aloud as 'tight and short' scripts whose job is to jog the DM's memory, not to be recited.
claims.source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)
claims.quote: tight and short

claims.claim: DMDavid: boxed text entered D&D with Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan, written for the Origins '79 AD&D tournament to give 'a consistent play experience in a competitive environment'.
claims.source: DMDavid — Picturing the dungeon: boxed text (David Hartlage, 2012-11-15)

claims.claim: 'When most speakers read something aloud, their voice takes a different tone and cadence than when they speak extemporaneously', so attention wanders; boxed text also dwells on 'the color of the sunset'.
claims.source: DMDavid — Picturing the dungeon: boxed text (David Hartlage, 2012-11-15)
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence

claims.claim: Gnome Stew (2008): in the 1980s reading boxed text aloud was 'considered a cardinal sin' among GMs, who were expected to paraphrase; the author later found reading helped immersion; commenters: 'Short box text is fine, long box text is a challenge.'
claims.source: Gnome Stew — Hot Button: Reading the Boxed Text (Walt Ciechanowski, 2008-12-18)
claims.quote: considered a cardinal sin

claims.claim: DM's Workshop: practice reading text aloud between sessions and match pacing to conversational speech; boxed text is a tool to adapt, not a script to recite.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop — DM 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (2019-09-27)
